Before understanding what this idiom means, picture the physical image it comes from.

Imagine you are standing on a street. There is a building or a bend in the road in front of you. You cannot see what is on the other side yet — but it is very close. It is just around the corner. You only need to take a few more steps, and you will reach it.

This image is the heart of the idiom.
What the Idiom Actually Means

When people say something is "around the corner," they mean it is going to happen very soon. It is not here yet, but it is so close that it feels almost visible — just like something physically sitting around the bend of a road.

It is used to talk about time, not physical distance.

Simple definition: Something is "around the corner" when it is about to happen in the very near future.
How the Literal Connects to the Figurative

Think of it this way:

  • Physical corner → something is nearby in space
  • Idiomatic corner → something is nearby in time

The leap from space to time is natural. In everyday life, we often describe time using the language of space. We say "the future is ahead of us," "the past is behind us," or "a big event is coming." The idiom "around the corner" follows the same logic — if something is just around the corner, it is right there, almost within reach, just not quite here yet.
Examples in Sentences

Here are examples across different situations so you can see how naturally this idiom appears:

Seasons and Holidays:

  • "Winter is just around the corner — you should buy a warm coat soon."
  • "Christmas is around the corner, so the shops are getting very busy."

Personal life:

  • "Don't give up. Success is just around the corner."
  • "Her graduation is right around the corner — her family is already planning a party."

Business and Economy:

  • "Economists are saying that a recovery is around the corner."
  • "The launch of our new product is right around the corner."

Warnings:

  • "Exams are around the corner, so stop wasting time."
  • "The deadline is around the corner — we need to hurry."

In every example above, notice that the thing being talked about has not happened yet, but it is very close in time.
The Word "Just" and "Right" — Why They Are Added

You will very often hear people say:

  • "just around the corner"
  • "right around the corner"

These words are added for emphasis. They make the idiom even stronger, pushing the idea that the event is extremely close — almost here this very moment. Without these words, the idiom still works, but with them, the sense of urgency or nearness is stronger.

Think of it like this:

  • "Around the corner" = soon
  • "Just around the corner" = very soon, almost here
The Tone: Is It Always Positive?

No, not always. This is an important nuance.

Most of the time, the idiom is used for things that are positive or exciting — a holiday, a victory, a new beginning, spring after a long winter. The tone feels hopeful and encouraging.

Example: "Keep working hard — your breakthrough is just around the corner."

However, it can also be used neutrally or even negatively, especially when talking about something difficult or unwelcome that is approaching.

Example: "Don't relax yet — more trouble is around the corner."
Example: "Tax season is around the corner again."

So the idiom itself is neutral in nature — its positive or negative feeling comes entirely from what is said to be around the corner.
What the Idiom Does NOT Mean

It is important to be clear about what this idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean something is physically near in location. If your friend says "the bakery is around the corner," they probably mean it literally — that is not the idiom. Context tells you which meaning is being used.
  • It does not mean something is already happening. The thing is still in the future, even if very close. The moment it arrives, you would no longer use this phrase.
  • It does not always mean something will happen today or tomorrow. "Soon" is relative. Depending on context, "around the corner" could mean next week, next month, or the next season — but it always implies closeness compared to a larger timeframe.
How to Tell the Literal From the Idiomatic

Since the same phrase can be literal or idiomatic, you need to look at context.

  • Literal: "Turn left, and the pharmacy is around the corner." → Talking about physical location.
  • Idiomatic: "Spring is just around the corner." → Spring cannot literally be around a corner. This is clearly about time.

When the subject is a time-based event, season, or change, it is almost always the idiom.
Similar Idioms With the Same Meaning

It helps to know expressions that mean the same thing, so you can recognize the idea even when different words are used:

  • "On the horizon" — something is approaching, visible in the distance (like the horizon line)
  • "In the pipeline" — something is being prepared and will arrive soon
  • "Imminent" — a formal single word meaning about to happen very soon
  • "Coming up" — a casual way to say something is approaching
  • "At hand" — something is very near and almost ready
  • "Any day now" — something could arrive at any moment

Among these, "around the corner" is one of the most visual and memorable because of the concrete image it creates in your mind.
A Simple Memory Trick

Every time you hear or read "around the corner," close your eyes and picture yourself standing on a street. Something wonderful (or important) is just out of sight — past the bend. You cannot see it yet, but you know it is there, right on the other side. Just a few more steps.

That picture is exactly what the idiom means in time: something is so close, you almost have it.
Quick Summary

ConceptDetail

"Around the corner" is an idiom meaning something is going to happen very soon. It comes from the image of something being physically close, just past a bend in the road. It is used for seasons, events, changes, successes, and even problems. Adding "just" or "right" makes the nearness feel even stronger. It can be positive, neutral, or slightly negative depending on what is said to be arriving. The thing described has not happened yet but is about to.
